title: Nika riots
summary: In January 532 the Blue and Green circus factions united under the cry Nika after a botched execution and rioted in Constantinople, burning much of the city including Hagia Sophia. Justinian considered fleeing but, according to Procopius, Theodora urged him to stay. On 18 January Belisarius and Mundus trapped the crowd in the Hippodrome; Procopius reports more than 30,000 dead, Theophanes and the Chronicon Paschale 35,000.

uncertainty.note: Riot began 13 January 532; the Hippodrome massacre followed on 18 January.

where.modern_name: Hippodrome of Constantinople (Sultanahmet Square), Istanbul, Turkey
where.historical_name: Hippodrome of Constantinople, capital of the Roman (Byzantine) Empire under Justinian I

importance.justification: A riot that nearly toppled Justinian, destroyed the earlier Hagia Sophia and was followed by his large-scale rebuilding of the city.

audience_note: Describes the mass killing of a crowd trapped in the Hippodrome; the death figures are ancient claims.

related.because: Encyclopaedia Romana says the fires set during the riot destroyed the earlier church of Hagia Sophia, which was rebuilt and consecrated five years later.

sources.title: The Nika Riots of 532 AD: The Revolt That Nearly Toppled Justinian

reviewer_note: Death figures are ancient claims attributed to Procopius (more than thirty thousand) and to Theophanes and the Chronicon Paschale (thirty-five thousand); Encyclopaedia Romana also notes Theodora's speech is likely a rhetorical set-piece. Byzantine Culture attributes the 30,000 figure to Procopius but gives it as "some 30,000 rioters". No person record for Justinian exists in the atlas, so none is linked.
